Seiko is a Japanese manufacturer of timing, measurement, and display systems for
sport, based in Tokyo. The equipment is made and sold by Seiko Time Creation Inc., a
subsidiary of Seiko Group Corporation, the holding company that traces its origins to
the watch shop Kintarō Hattori opened in 1881.[^overview][^grouplist][^hattori] Seiko
is named among the manufacturers of aquatic timing systems, with
[Colorado Time Systems](colorado-time-systems.md),
[Swiss Timing](swiss-timing.md) (Omega) and
[Daktronics](daktronics.md),[^watiming] though its record at international
championships is documented mainly in athletics rather than in aquatics.

The Seiko hardware documented in the [equipment reference](../equipment/index.md) is
the swimming start-signal equipment built around the company's electronic start sound
generators.

## History

The company that makes the timing equipment is older than its present name. It was
founded in 1966 as Goko, a sales agency for K. Hattori and Co.'s facility clocks, and
incorporated in 1970. It was renamed Goko Time System in 1984 and Seiko
C.S.T. in 1990, and became a wholly owned subsidiary in 1993. It took over the
facility-clock business in 1997, and in 1998 took over the sports timing and
measurement business from Seiko Corporation, at which point it was renamed Seiko Time
Systems. Manufacturing and maintenance followed from Seiko Precision in 2005, and
timing-support services from the group holding company in 2014.[^history]

Seiko Time Creation Inc. was formed on 1 April 2021, when Seiko Time Systems and Seiko
Clock Inc. were brought together. Seiko describes the event as a management
integration rather than a merger and does not say which company survived in law,
though the new company keeps Seiko Time Systems' 1970 establishment date and its whole
chronology.[^merger][^history] The company's web address moved from `seiko-sts.co.jp`
to `seiko-stc.co.jp` with the change of name, and the old domain still redirects.

The combined company has since been narrowed back to time systems. It transferred its
factory-automation business in 2024, and its clock business to Seiko Watch Corporation
in two stages, sales in April 2025 and the clock technology division in April
2026.[^history][^clock2026] Its headcount fell accordingly, from 390 at formation to
195 as of 1 April 2026, when it had capital of ¥500 million and was headed by Takeshi
Ichikawa from offices in Kōtō, Tokyo.[^merger][^overview]

Three companies in the wider group are easy to confuse, and the distinction matters
when reading patents and product literature. Seiko Time Creation makes the timing
equipment. Seiko Instruments Inc. is a separate subsidiary working in electronic and
precision components, and is the assignee of the swimming-timing patents cited
elsewhere on this wiki. Seiko Group Corporation, renamed from Seiko Holdings
Corporation on 1 October 2022, is the parent of both.[^grouplist][^rename] Seiko Epson
Corporation, despite the name, is not part of that group at all: it is separately
listed and independently run, sharing the Hattori origins and a cross-shareholding of
about 3 %, and it remains a major movement supplier to Seiko Watch
Corporation.[^grouplist][^epson]

## Products

Seiko Time Creation sells facility clocks, sports timing and measurement equipment,
digital signage, large display boards and baseball scoreboards, and provides timing
support services at sporting events.[^overview]

- Swimming, a system built around the `PS-1400` electronic start sound generator and
  the `PT-9000` printing timer, with starting blocks carrying relay take-off sensors,
  touch plates, per-lane lane boxes, underwater video, a light-stimulus start signal
  system for swimmers with a hearing impairment, and scoreboards.[^catalogue]
- Athletics, photo-finish systems, the `PS-200` start signal generator and its
  loud-hailer sets, track timers, photobeam units, wind gauges and field
  equipment.[^rikujyo]
- Multi-timing, a portable line of sports printers, timers and electronic starters
  usable across sports.[^rikujyo]

Individual Seiko products are catalogued in the
[equipment reference](../equipment/index.md): the swimming
[start sound generators](../equipment/swimming/starter/seiko-ps-1400.md), whose current
model is the `PS-1400` and which replaced the
[PS-1300](../equipment/swimming/starter/seiko-ps-1300.md) and before it the much larger
[PS-1200](../equipment/swimming/starter/seiko-ps-1200.md); and the portable
cross-sport
[Electronic Starting System](../equipment/swimming/starter/seiko-electronic-starting-system.md),
whose earlier generations are the
[PS-105](../equipment/swimming/starter/seiko-ps-105.md),
[PS-107](../equipment/swimming/starter/seiko-ps-107.md) and
[PS-109](../equipment/swimming/starter/seiko-ps-109.md); and the two touch plates, the
[AQUA type](../equipment/swimming/touchpad/seiko-aqua-touch-plate.md) and the narrower
[full-frame type](../equipment/swimming/touchpad/seiko-full-frame-touch-plate.md).
Timers and scoreboards are added as those pages are written.

## In swim timing

Seiko's swimming equipment is sold as a certified system rather than as separate
parts. The company states that the starter, the starting blocks, the backstroke ledge,
the lane boxes, the
[AQUA-type touch plate](../equipment/swimming/touchpad/seiko-aqua-touch-plate.md) and
the printing timer conform to World
Aquatics rules and are certified Class AA and Class A by the Japan Swimming Federation.
The certification is not uniform across the range: the
[1,900 mm full-frame touch plate](../equipment/swimming/touchpad/seiko-full-frame-touch-plate.md)
carries Japan Swimming Federation Class A alone, with no World Aquatics
line.[^catalogue] The [start-systems overview](../equipment/swimming/starter/index.md)
covers the governing-body requirements those certifications answer to.

Seiko sells starters on both sides of that line. The deck generators are swimming
equipment and carry the certifications; the portable Electronic Starting System is
listed in the athletics catalogue as general multi-timing equipment and carries
none.[^catalogue][^rikujyo]

## In competition

Seiko's timekeeping record is documented most fully in athletics rather than in
aquatics. World Athletics states that Seiko has been its choice at major championships
since 1985, that it has supplied timing and measurement to more than 190 World
Athletics events, and that it had served continuously as official timer for seventeen
consecutive championships up to and including Oregon in 2022.[^wa][^waoregon] Seiko
dates the run from the second championships, at Rome in 1987, and puts the event count
at more than 180 rather than 190.[^seikosports]

Seiko's own history also lists it as official timekeeper of the Olympic Games at Tokyo
in 1964, Sapporo in 1972, Barcelona in 1992, Lillehammer in 1994, Nagano in 1998 and
Salt Lake City in 2002, with no later entry.[^seikosports]

In aquatics its work is mainly domestic. The Japan Swimming Federation lists Seiko on
its own sponsor page as an official timekeeping partner, and Seiko says it is the sole
such partner and dates the relationship to 2003, neither of which the federation's page
states.[^jasf][^seikosports][^catalogue] Seiko supports the Japanese domestic calendar,
including the Japan Swimming Championships, the National Sports Festival, the national
school championships and the Japan Open.[^catalogue]

Seiko timed the swimming at the 2001 World Aquatics Championships in Fukuoka, the only
edition it is known to have timed, and the touchpads malfunctioned repeatedly across
the eight days of competition. Times had to be corrected from backup timing or video
evidence, and the system recorded an early take-off of minus 0.06 s that disqualified
the United States women's 4 × 200 m freestyle relay on a successful British protest.
The disqualification stood, and the governing body, then FINA, instead awarded the
United States a second set of gold medals without changing the official result. It
defended the equipment, saying it had a fine reputation and that swimmers had to strike
the pads in the right way, then signed a three-event deal with Swiss Timing covering the
2002 world short-course championships in Moscow and the 2003 and 2005 championships in
Barcelona and Montreal.[^sw2001][^wp2001]

Omega has been an official partner of World Aquatics since 1973, and timed the 2023
championships when they returned to Fukuoka.[^omega][^wt2023]
